question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

options.opc: Complete loss of taste to the tongue

paths: (Facial nerve structure)-PART_OF->(Bone structure of cranium)-LOCATION_OF->(Neurologic Examination)-DIAGNOSES->(Aphasia, Expressive)

enhanced_information: The patient's right-sided facial weakness and drooping, with intact sensation and no other neurological deficits, suggests a peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, likely Bell's palsy, rather than a central cause like a stroke. In Bell's palsy, the entire side of the face is affected, including the forehead, which would not wrinkle. This aligns with the finding of a smooth forehead, not a wrinkled one. The facial nerve also innervates the lacrimal and salivary glands, so decreased salivation is a plausible additional finding. Partial hearing loss can occur due to the proximity of the facial nerve to the auditory structures, but it is less common. Complete loss of taste to the tongue is unlikely, as the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve typically affects taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not complete loss. Expressive aphasia is related to central brain lesions, not peripheral nerve issues, and is thus irrelevant here. Therefore, decreased salivation is the most likely additional finding in this patient, consistent with facial nerve involvement in Bell's palsy.
